---
title: "Nonprehensile Manipulation"
description: "Planning through contact: when the planner must invent the contact sequence, not just track one."
---

::: {.research-page}

::: {.research-lead}
When a robot cannot grasp an object, the plan *is* the sequence of contacts.
:::

Pushing, toppling, pivoting, and re-acquiring an object are all cases in which
the robot never closes a rigid grasp. The object moves because contacts are
made and broken in the right order, and the hard part of the problem is
deciding that order. A trajectory optimizer cannot recover from a contact
sequence that was wrong to begin with.

Our work asks a specific question: **what should the discrete object be, if the
planner is expected to invent contacts that do not exist yet?**

## Planning through contact

::: {.research-paper}

**Planar build**

[Planar Build →](planar-build/index.qmd) — the current construction on the
planar step scene, by topic: contact states, edits, the hold gate and its
certificates, the local solver and the search, with figures, an interactive
viewer, and the open issues.

**Results**

[Results →](results/index.qmd): the planner lifts the box onto the step from
rest, held at every instant, at each disk friction of the declared band, given
the lift's formation sequence; with videos.

:::

The construction has five pieces:

- **Formations.** Every body carries a finite, named inventory of features
  (edges and convex vertices). A candidate contact (a *template*) is a pair of
  features on two bodies with a signed gap, defined whether or not the pair
  touches. A *formation* is the set of templates in principal contact, in the
  sense of Xiao and Ji, recognized from a pose with small tolerances; it is
  the discrete state, carried alongside the continuous pose.
- **Edits.** Neighbouring formations differ by making, breaking or
  transferring one contact; several change at once only when no single change
  is possible (the pivot). A transport moves the object without changing
  contacts.
- **The hold gate.** Before an edit is tried, a linear program checks that
  the contacts that persist through it can hold the object against gravity,
  within the manipulator's actuator limits, at a pose where the change can
  happen. In its idealized form it never discards a realizable edit, and an
  interval version certifies the hold over whole regions of poses.
- **Realization.** A local solver, a quasi-static realizer that plans on the
  edit's known contacts and tracks the plan in simulation, either realizes the
  edit or reports why it failed.
- **Search.** A search over edits, ordered by a ranker and a value estimate,
  counts the expensive solver calls, with the number of calls bounded by the
  ranker's probabilities.

The hold gate is what forbids a manipulator from letting go mid-topple, and
admits the same release once the object rests on other contacts.

## Why unmade contacts matter

Complementarity-based planners enumerate velocity modes over the contacts that
collision detection has already found, and graphs of convex sets place modes on
vertices that must be enumerated in advance. Both are effective for reasoning
about contacts a robot already has. Neither can express *go and establish
contact with that edge*, because the contact is not in the state until it
exists.

Here every contact the geometry allows is a named template with a gap defined
before it touches, so *make that contact* is an edge of the graph from the
start. That is the one structural difference, and everything else in the
construction follows from it.

## Status

On a proof-of-concept task, lifting a box onto a step with a disk too weak
to carry it, the lift in which the box is held at every instant, the
*indirect lift*, has its last four edits and closing transport certified for
every disk friction in a declared band. Given only that lift's formation
sequence, the planner realizes it in simulation from rest at the band's
frictions ([Results](results/index.qmd)). Finding the sequence from the scene
alone is open and is the next work. The
[planar build](planar-build/index.qmd) pages give the details, and
[Issues](planar-build/issues.qmd) the open work.
